questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6y-x).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=6y-x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=6y-x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=6\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-1\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-6\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=-6\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1.$

questions.problem:
By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+1}{\int }_{{e}^{y-1}}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225558/assets/314b881b95ea804456b3e41a1d8fec70cf459e007e2120d9018e3bef02f1b523.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 3\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+1,\,{e}^{y-1}\le x\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x={e}^{y-1}\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225558/assets/c9b097164e2b5215a051e18de055f3cce4c26600caf510bc3b0071b77b645089.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+1}{\int }_{{e}^{y-1}}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=4u+7v+2,\,y=u+2v+1.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-7y+3,\,v=by+cx-2,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4u+7v+2 \\ u+2v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4u+7v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 4-7\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x-2)+(-7)\cdot (y-1) \\ (-1)\cdot (x-2)+4\cdot (y-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-7y+3 \\ 4y-x-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-7y+3,\,v=4y+(-1)x-2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+4+(-1)=5.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $10?$

I. ${R}_{10}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $10$

II. ${\text{M}}_{5}(R)$, the vector space of all $5\times 5$ matrices over $R$

III. ${R}^{10}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}_{10}[t])=10+1=11\ne 10.\,\times 
  $$

II. Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(\text{R}))={n}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({\text{M}}_{5}(R))={5}^{2}=25\ne 10.\,\times 
  $$

III. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{10})=10.\,✓
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: On a busy waterway, barges pass by a particular point continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate of one every $10$ minutes. Determine the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one. Round your answer to four decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since barges pass continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time between two successive barges using an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the amount of time between two successive barges. Since a barge passes every $10$ minutes, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ barges per minute.

The time interval between two successive barges can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<X<7) & ={\int }_{5}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{7}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/10}{|}_{5}^{7} \\  & =-{e}^{-7/10}+{e}^{-5/10} \\  & ≈0.1099\end{aligned}
$$
